names.name: divyaṃ janma karma ca (divine birth and action)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Though unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, Kṛṣṇa comes into being (saṃbhavāmi) through his own māyā, presiding over his own prakṛti (4.6); whenever dharma declines and adharma rises he sends himself forth (4.7), age after age, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (4.8); he has had many births, all of which he knows (4.5); whoever knows his birth and action as divine is not reborn but comes to him (4.9). The word avatāra itself does not occur.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The noun bhakti does not occur, but Arjuna is taught as the Lord's devotee (bhakta) and friend (4.3); the Lord responds to people in the way they resort to him (4.11); many absorbed in him and taking refuge in him reached his state (4.10); the meditator sits with thought on him and intent on him (6.14); the yogin established in oneness worships him as abiding in all beings (6.31); and of all yogins the one who worships him with faith, inner self gone to him, is the most yoked (6.47).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: whoever knows the Lord as unstained by actions is not bound by actions (4.14); the one content with what comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, the same in success and failure, is not bound even when acting (4.22); actions do not bind the self-possessed one who has renounced actions by yoga and cut doubt by knowledge (4.41); the constant renouncer, free of the pairs, is easily released from bondage (5.3); the unyoked one, attached to the fruit through desire, is bound (5.12).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The goal named in 5.24–26: the yogin whose happiness, delight and light are within, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24); seers with impurities destroyed, dualities cut, self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings attain it (5.25); for self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger it is near on every side (5.26). Related expressions in ch. 6: peace culminating in nirvāṇa that abides in the Lord (6.15), becoming Brahman and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Brahman is every factor of the sacrifice and is what is to be reached (4.24); it is the fire into which sacrifice is offered (4.25); the eternal Brahman is reached by those who eat the remainder of sacrifice (4.31); the yoked sage soon reaches it (5.6); actions are placed in it (5.10); it is flawless and the same, so that those whose mind rests in sameness are established in it (5.19–20); the yogin becomes Brahman (brahma-bhūta) and attains brahma-nirvāṇa and contact with Brahman (5.24, 6.27–28).

name: The Lord's action without need

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord made the fourfold class order by the division of guṇa and karma, yet is to be known as its non-doer (akartṛ), imperishable (4.13); actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit, and whoever knows him thus is not bound by actions (4.14); knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation acted (4.15).

notes: Chs. 4–6 contribution, from extractor A's cpt:akartrtva (the Lord's side).

name: The Lord's reciprocity: as one approaches, so one is received (BhG 4.11)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.11: in whatever way people approach the Lord, in that way he receives them; humans follow his path in every way.

notes: Commentators read the second line either as all paths being finally the Lord's or as people following his example (cf. 3.23).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Being the same in success and failure (4.22); neither hating nor craving (5.3); seeing a learned brahmin, cow, elephant, dog and dog-eater with an equal eye (5.18); the mind established in sameness, as Brahman is the same (5.19); neither rejoicing at the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant (5.20); composure amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); clod, stone and gold alike (6.8); equal regard toward friend, foe, neutral, good and wicked (6.9); seeing the same everywhere (6.29), by comparison with oneself (6.32). Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'yoga as sāmya' (6.33).

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Arjuna asks what becomes of one with faith who does not strive enough and whose mind falls from yoga before perfection — does he perish like a torn cloud, fallen from both (6.37–39)? Kṛṣṇa: there is no destruction for him here or hereafter, for no doer of good goes to a bad end (6.40); he dwells for endless years in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn in a pure and prosperous house (6.41), or — rarer — in a family of wise yogins (6.42); there he regains the understanding of his former body and strives again (6.43), carried on by his former practice even against his will; even the mere enquirer into yoga passes beyond śabda-brahman (6.44); striving, cleansed, perfected through many births, he reaches the highest course (6.45).

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord declared the imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, Vivasvat told it to Manu and Manu to Ikṣvāku (4.1); received thus in succession (paramparā) it was known by the royal sages, and over a long time it was lost here (4.2); the Lord declares the same ancient yoga to Arjuna because he is his devotee and friend, for it is the highest secret (4.3). Knowledge is to be learned from the knowers who have seen the truth, approached with prostration, thorough questioning and service; they will teach it (4.34).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Knowledge is to be learnt from 'the knowers who see the truth' (jñāninas tattvadarśinaḥ), approached with prostration, thorough questioning and service; they will instruct it (4.34). The teaching itself is presented as passed down in succession from Kṛṣṇa (4.1–3). The word guru does not occur in these verses.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.25–30 carries the language of the fire-offering over to inner disciplines: the senses offered into the fires of restraint, sense objects into the fires of the senses, the activities of senses and breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge, prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is unborn, of imperishable self and lord of beings, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6); he responds to people as they resort to him (4.11); he made the fourfold class-order yet is the imperishable non-doer (4.13); actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit (4.14); he is the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings (5.29); he is seen everywhere and everything in him (6.30). Whether the 'lord' (prabhu, vibhu) of 5.14–15, who creates no agency and takes on no one's merit or sin, is the supreme Lord or the embodied self is disputed by commentators.

name: Desire (and anger) as the enemy (BhG 3.36–43)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: desire and anger recur as a pair to be overcome: one who can withstand here, before release from the body, the surge (vega) that arises from desire and anger is yoked and a happy person (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near on every side for ascetics freed from desire and anger (5.26).

notes: Chs. 4–6 contribution, from extractor A's obstacle entry obs:kama-the-enemy for 5.23 and 5.26 (continuing 3.37–43).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The course of action is deep (4.17); action binds when done from desire with attachment to fruit (5.12), but not when done without attachment, for the sake of sacrifice, with actions placed in Brahman (4.20–23, 5.10); knowledge burns all actions to ashes (4.19, 4.37); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32) and all action culminates in knowledge (4.33); the Lord is not stained by actions and whoever knows this is not bound (4.14).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even sages are bewildered about what action and inaction are (4.16); one must understand action (karma), vikarma and inaction (akarma), for the course of action is deep (4.17); the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18). The text does not define vikarma.

relations.note: the analysis of action announced in 4.16–18

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: chs. 4–6 name the goal in several ways: not being born again and coming to the Lord (4.9); release from the inauspicious (4.16); going to the eternal Brahman (4.31, 5.6); supreme peace (4.39, 5.12, 5.29); non-return (apunarāvṛtti, 5.17); brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24–26); being forever free (sadā mukta) while intent on mokṣa (5.28); peace culminating in nirvāṇa (6.15); the highest course (parā gati, 6.45).

name: The body as the city of nine gates (navadvāra pura)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Having renounced all actions by the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).

notes: The same image occurs in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18 (navadvāre pure dehī).

name: Action without attachment to its fruit

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire and intention (4.19); abandoning attachment to the fruit, ever content, dependent on nothing (4.20); acting for the sake of sacrifice, action dissolves (4.23); acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment, one is unstained like a lotus leaf (5.10); yogins act for self-purification (5.11); the yoked one abandons the fruit and gains peace, the unyoked is bound by attachment to it (5.12); the true renunciant and yogin does the required action without depending on its fruit (6.1).

name: The self is not the agent; the guṇas act

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: having abandoned attachment to the fruit, though fully engaged in action one does nothing at all (4.20); the yoked knower of reality thinks 'I do nothing at all' while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, releasing, grasping and opening and closing the eyes, holding that the senses move among the objects of the senses (5.8–9); having renounced all actions with the mind, the embodied one dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13); the master (prabhu) creates neither agency nor actions nor the link of action with its fruit — inherent nature (svabhāva) is at work — and the pervading, mighty one (vibhu) takes on no one's sin or good deed (5.14–15). Whether prabhu and vibhu name the embodied self or the Lord is disputed by the commentators.

notes: Chs. 4–6 contribution, from extractor A's cpt:akartrtva (the knower's side). In these chapters the text says the senses, or svabhāva, act (not, as in 3.27–28, the guṇas).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have both passed through many births, which Kṛṣṇa knows and Arjuna does not (4.5); whoever knows the Lord's divine birth and action does not go to rebirth on leaving the body (4.9); the one fallen from yoga dwells in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn, carrying the understanding and practice of his former body (6.41–44), perfected through many births (6.45).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Asked whether renunciation of actions or yoga is better (5.1), Kṛṣṇa says both bring the highest good but the yoga of action is superior (5.2); the constant renouncer is one who neither hates nor craves (5.3); Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one in result (5.4–5); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6); renouncing all actions by the mind the embodied one dwells at ease (5.13); the renouncer and yogin is one who does required action without depending on its fruit, not one without sacred fires or rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga, for no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2).

name: The self as its own friend and enemy (BhG 6.5–6)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 6.5–6: one should raise the self by the self and not let it sink; the self alone is the self's friend and the self alone its enemy — friend to the one who has conquered himself, while for the one not self-possessed the self acts with hostility like an enemy.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 5.20 describes the knower of Brahman in the same terms as the steady-wise of 2.54–72: not elated by the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant, steady in intellect (sthira-buddhi), undeluded, established in Brahman.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The self in which, by knowledge, all beings are seen, and then in the Lord (4.35); the yoked yogin sees the self abiding in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29), his self having become the self of all beings (5.7); restrained thought (citta) rests in the self alone (6.18) and, seeing the self by the self, is content in the self (6.20). The same word is used reflexively: one raises oneself by oneself, and the self is one's own friend or enemy (6.5–6). In 4.35 and 6.29 'ātmani' can also be read reflexively ('in oneself').

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: chs. 4–6 name the guṇas only in passing: the fourfold class-order was made according to the division of guṇas and actions (4.13); the yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has rajas stilled (6.27).

name: The twofold commitment (dvividhā niṣṭhā): jñāna-yoga and karma-yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the childish, not the learned, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as separate; one properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both; the place reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by those of Yoga too, and whoever sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees (5.4–5). In context (5.1–6; cf. 3.3) Sāṃkhya stands with the renunciation of actions and knowledge, Yoga with the yoga of action.

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya) was created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma; though its maker, he is a non-doer. The verse does not say whether the division is fixed by birth or by conduct.

name: Sacrifice reinterpreted (yajña)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4.24–33 list the sacrifices offered by different practitioners, all born of action and all purifying: every element of the offering seen as Brahman; sacrifice to the gods; offering sacrifice by sacrifice into the fire of Brahman; offering the senses into the fires of restraint; offering sense objects into the fires of the senses; offering the activities of the senses and of breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint; sacrifice with material things, with austerity, with yoga, with study and with knowledge; offering prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, with breath-regulation; offering the breaths into the breaths with regulated food. The sacrifice of knowledge is the best, since all action culminates in knowledge.

members: every factor of the rite seen as Brahman (brahmārpaṇa, 4.24)
sacrifice offered by sacrifice into the fire of Brahman (4.25b)
the senses offered into the fires of restraint (4.26a)
sense-objects offered into the fires of the senses (4.26b)
actions of senses and breath offered into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge (4.27)
sacrifice of recitation and of knowledge (svādhyāya-, jñāna-yajña, 4.28)
prāṇa offered into apāna and apāna into prāṇa by those intent on prāṇāyāma (4.29)
breaths offered into breaths by those regulated in food (4.30)
